newsitem.title: UK: London analysts greet Amersham surprise.
newsitem.headline: London analysts greet Amersham surprise.

text.p: Analysts in London welcomed the planned merger of British health technology group Amersham International Plc with Norway's Nycomed ASA as a strong strategic fit on Tuesday, but were struggling to digest the financial implications of the move.

News of the agreement came as a surprise, with many analysts still coming to terms with Amersham's June 10 announcement that its was to merge its life sciences business with Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc's Pharmacia Biotech.
To complicate the picture even further, Amersham raised its stake in its Japanese nuclear medicines joint venture, Nihon-Medi Physics, to 50 percent only last October.
"It is one of those things that people thought could happen, but it is still a surprise," said an analyst with a UK bank brokerage.

Kleinwort Benson analyst Stuart Harris added: "It was obvious that Nycomed was going to do something, but it was a surprise from Amersham's point of view because it was so hot on the heels of the Amersham/Biotech deal."

Harris said the agreement between Nycomed and the British company was much more logical than a failed 1995 attempt by Nycomed, then part of drugs and energy combine Hafslund Nycomed, to merge with U.S. generic drug group Ivax Corp.

"This makes absolutely perfect sense," Harris said, stressing the benefit to Amersham of Nycomed's established distribution network in North America and Amersham's strong sales position in Japan, where Nycomed currently has a distribution accord with Daiichi Pharmaceutical Co Ltd.
The combined Nycomed Amersham will be world leader in nuclear imaging and x-ray imaging products used in diagnosis, and number two in less significant magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) field.

The UK bank brokerage analyst, however, was more cautious about the benefits of getting together. He said Nycomed had serious problems with its traditional x-ray imaging products, where intense pressure on prices in the U.S. hit profits across the group last year.
And growth in use of ultrasound imaging, which Nycomed Amersham managers said could have total market sales of one billion stg by 2005, remained uncertain, he added.
Kleinwort's Harris, however, said "we have a lot of faith in the Amersham management, I think they are astute people. They must believe the corner has turned in the x-ray imaging market."

On ultrasound, where the injection of small bubbles into the body offers the potential for much simpler, cheaper and safer scanning of organs like the heart, liver and kidneys, Harris said: "there is a logic for the market going that big, but we have to see if the products on the market and to be launched can take up that opportunity."

However, analysts were struggling to calculate the impact of the latest merger on earnings for the combined group. One said the effect could be "enormously earnings enhancing," with rises in earnings per share of around a third possible.
Another said Nycomed Amersham could have earnings per share of anywhere between 100 and 140 pence in 1998.
Analysts are having to calculate two sets of merger costs and cost savings, plus the effect of a switch by the combined Nycomed Amersham to calendar year reporting.

In addition one said the foreign exchange position, already complicated at Amersham, becomes "an even bigger nightmare," with manufacturing and sales spread across Scandinavia, Britain, Japan and the U.S.
